prompt: Put the layers of a self-hosted model in order, from the bottom to the one your program calls.
trap: The runtime loads the weights, so the weights sit below it.

prompt: Which single number decides whether a model runs on a given machine at all?

choices.text: The number of processor cores
choices.why: Cores matter for some runtimes; they do not decide whether the weights fit.

choices.text: The speed of the network connection to the machine
choices.why: The network carries requests; it does not hold the model.

choices.text: Accelerator memory
choices.why: Right. Weights that do not fit do not run, or run from slower memory.

choices.text: The size of the disk the weights are stored on
choices.why: A disk stores them; generation reads them from memory.

prompt: A self-hosted model passes a health check that sends 'hello' every minute, yet fails on some real e-mails. Which cause does section 07 describe?
hint: What does a long prompt need that a short one does not?

choices.text: The model refuses e-mails that contain addresses
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson suggests a refusal.

choices.text: Memory runs out on long prompts while short ones still fit
choices.why: Right. The cache grows with the prompt, and 'hello' never grows it.

choices.text: The health check uses up the rate limit
choices.why: A self-hosted server has no rate limit unless you add one.

choices.text: The runtime only supports English
choices.why: Languages belong to the model, not the runtime.

prompt: A model has 8 billion parameters stored at 16 bits each. How many gigabytes do the weights take?
The same 8-billion-parameter model is quantised to 4 bits. How many gigabytes do the weights take now?
Why is '8B' in a model's name not the exact number of parameters?

choices.why: Right, and the exact number follows from the published architecture.

choices.text: It counts only the layers that are trained
choices.why: Every parameter is trained; the name is a rounding.

choices.text: It counts tokens in the training data, in billions
choices.why: The card gives about 15 trillion tokens of training data, a different number.

choices.text: Providers round it up for marketing, and the true count is much lower than the label
choices.why: The true count is slightly higher, and it was rounded, not inflated.

prompt: Llama 3.1 8B needs 128 KiB of KV cache per token. Four requests of 8,192 tokens are served at once. What does the cache add to the 4 GB of 4-bit weights?
hint: 1 GiB per request of that length.

choices.text: Nothing: the cache lives on the disk
choices.why: It is held in accelerator memory, beside the weights.

choices.text: 1 GiB, shared by the four requests
choices.why: Each request being served needs its own cache.

choices.text: About 4 GiB, as much again as the weights
choices.why: Right. At long contexts and several users, the cache rivals the model.

choices.text: 128 KiB, since the cache is per token and not per request
choices.why: It is per token of every request: 128 KiB times 8,192 times four.

prompt: What is quantisation?

choices.text: Training a smaller model to imitate a larger one
choices.why: That is distillation, which lesson 2 met in R1's distills.

choices.text: Storing the same weights with less precision
choices.why: Right. 16-bit numbers become 8- or 4-bit ones.

choices.text: Removing the layers that contribute least
choices.why: That is pruning; quantisation keeps every weight.

choices.text: Splitting a model across several machines so each holds part of it
choices.why: That shares the memory load without changing precision.

prompt: Which of ana's tasks is most at risk from a 4-bit quantised model, and why?

choices.text: Sorting, because five labels need more precision than three
choices.why: The number of labels is not what precision affects.

choices.text: Drafting replies, because long text uses more memory
choices.why: Memory is about fitting; this question is about quality.

choices.text: Extraction, since exact JSON is a precise format
choices.why: Right. Strict formats are among the first things to suffer, so they are what to check.

choices.text: None of them: four bits loses nothing
choices.why: Four bits loses a little, unevenly.

prompt: How should a 4-bit version of a model ana is evaluating appear in lesson 5's evaluation?

choices.text: It inherits the 16-bit score, as the weights are the same
choices.why: They are the same weights at different precision, which can change answers.

choices.text: As its own row, with its own score
choices.why: Right. It is only cheaper if its score is still good enough.

choices.text: It is left out, because quantised models cannot be evaluated against an API
choices.why: Any model that answers can be evaluated.

choices.text: As a footnote to the 16-bit row
choices.why: A footnote hides exactly the difference that matters.

prompt: Why does generation speed for a single request depend mostly on memory bandwidth?
hint: What is read for every token?

choices.text: Because tokens are stored in memory before being sent
choices.why: A few tokens are tiny; the weights are not.

choices.text: Because the prompt is copied in for every token
choices.why: The cache exists precisely to avoid that.

choices.text: Because arithmetic on accelerators is slow
choices.why: The arithmetic is quick; the waiting is for data.

choices.text: Every weight is read once per new token
choices.why: Right, so speed is roughly bandwidth over the size of the weights.

prompt: With 2,000 GB/s of memory bandwidth, what is the ceiling in tokens per second for a model whose weights take 40 GB?
hint: Bandwidth divided by the size of the weights.

prompt: A server batches requests. What happens to total throughput and to each request's speed?
hint: The weights are read once per step for everyone.

choices.text: More tokens a second in all; each one a little slower
choices.why: Right, which is how a busy machine becomes cheap per token.

choices.text: Both rise, since the weights are read less often
choices.why: Each request now shares each step with others.

choices.text: Both fall, because the batch has to wait for its slowest member
choices.why: Total throughput is what batching raises.

choices.text: Nothing changes; batching only saves memory
choices.why: Batching changes throughput, at some cost in memory.

prompt: A request costs $69 per million requests through an API, and a machine costs $1,500 a month. How many requests a month make them cost the same? Answer in millions, to one decimal place.
In section 06, what is real and what is the course's assumption?
hint: Which numbers came from a capture?

choices.text: The prices are assumed; the volume of e-mail is measured
choices.why: It is the other way round for both.

choices.text: Token counts and prices are real; volume and machine cost are assumed
choices.why: Right, and the lesson says which is which beside each number.

choices.text: Everything is measured on Lantern Books' real traffic
choices.why: Lantern Books does not exist; its volume is an assumption.

choices.text: Everything is an assumption
choices.why: The token counts were made by a real tokenizer and the prices read from the sheet.

prompt: ana's drafting task sends a 2,000-token prompt and gets 300 tokens back. Compared with sorting, what happens to the break-even volume for a machine?
hint: Cost per request, then the division.

choices.text: It rises, because long replies are slower
choices.why: Speed is not in the break-even sum; cost per request is.

choices.text: It stays the same, since the machine's cost is fixed
choices.why: The API side of the comparison changes.

choices.text: It doubles, because there are two tasks now
choices.why: The number of tasks is not the factor.

choices.text: It falls, by as much as the cost per request rises
choices.why: Right. Dearer requests make a machine pay for itself at a lower volume.

prompt: Which of these become your job when you self-host? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Patching the runtime and the drivers
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Adding capacity when the load grows
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Answering when it stops on a Sunday
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Retraining the model every month
choices.why: Nothing requires retraining; a model on disk stays as it is.

prompt: Why does a self-hosted machine have to be sized for the peak rather than the average?

choices.text: Because runtimes refuse to start below a minimum load
choices.why: Runtimes start fine with nothing to do.

choices.text: Its capacity is fixed, and the load comes in bunches
choices.why: Right. An API provider's fleet absorbs the bunch; one machine has what it has.

choices.text: Because the price per hour rises with use
choices.why: A machine costs the same per hour, busy or idle.

choices.text: Because the weights grow during busy periods and shrink again once the load has passed
choices.why: The weights do not change size.

prompt: A hospital's records may not leave its building. Its volume is small and the arithmetic favours an API. What does section 08 say?

choices.text: Use the API: the arithmetic decides
choices.why: One row that truly applies outweighs the arithmetic.

choices.text: Self-host; the requirement decides
choices.why: Right. Section 07's work becomes the price of a requirement.

choices.text: Use an open model from a host, which keeps data in
choices.why: A host receives the data.

choices.text: Wait until volume grows enough to justify a machine
choices.why: Volume is not the row that applies here.

prompt: Match each situation to the reason in section 08 that it falls under.

pairs.left: A ship's system with no connection at sea
A contract forbids sending text to third parties
The model must not change until the team decides
A fine-tuned model no host offers

prompt: Which middle path keeps the data in an account Lantern Books controls without running the machine itself?

choices.text: An open model from a third-party host
choices.why: The data goes to the host.

choices.text: A closed model on its maker's global route
choices.why: That sends the data wherever there is capacity.

choices.text: A dedicated deployment in its own cloud account
choices.why: Right. Somebody else runs it; the data stays in an account it controls.

choices.text: A quantised model on a laptop
choices.why: That is self-hosting, machine and all.

prompt: The cache a runtime keeps so it does not recompute the prompt for every new token is called the ___ cache.
hint: Two letters: what it stores for each token.
